variants.name: std::promise / std::future / std::async (shared state)
variants.implementation_notes: C++11 ships both ends of the pair: std::promise is the write end - set_value or set_exception makes the shared state ready - and std::future is the read end, where get() blocks and wait_for/wait_until bound the wait; std::async and std::packaged_task produce futures from callables. A std::future is a unique reference to its shared state, so several consumers need std::shared_future, and the type is not co_awaitable - exactly the gap the coroutine and continuation variants fill. Use the classic pair for a single result consumed once and for bridging a computation to a thread that must wait.
variants.code_sketch:
std::promise<int> p;                              // write end (single assignment)
auto f = p.get_future();                          // read end given to the consumer
std::thread t([&p] { p.set_value(compute()); });   // or set_exception on failure
int v = f.get();                                  // blocks once; f is invalid after
t.join();
pitfalls: std::future is move-only and single-reader: a second get() throws std::future_error (no_state) and the value cannot be waited for twice - share via std::shared_future instead.

A std::promise destroyed without setting a value makes its future ready with broken_promise, and destroying the last reference to an async-created shared state may block until the task finishes - an abandoned std::async future stalls scope exit.

variants.name: C++20 coroutines: co_await on a task type
variants.idiom_name: co_await / co_return state machine over a task type
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 coroutines turn the consuming side into ordinary control flow: co_await suspends the coroutine until the awaited task is ready, replacing the blocking get() and the callback chain, while the task type's promise object is the write end that the coroutine machinery resumes through. The standard library's own awaitable task arrives later, so until then the task type and its executor come from a framework - choose this variant when the toolchain is C++20 and the manual shared-state plumbing of std::future is the pain point.
pitfalls: Coroutine frames are heap-allocated and the task type decides who resumes them: a task nobody awaits leaks its frame, and references living across co_await are the top lifetime bug class.
std::future and std::promise are not awaitable - mixing the std pair with coroutines means writing adapters instead of sharing a handle.

variants.name: Continuation futures (folly::Future chains on an Executor)
variants.idiom_name: folly::Future + thenValue/thenTry with an explicit Executor
variants.implementation_notes: Continuation-style futures exist because std::future is anemic: folly::Future attaches callbacks with thenValue or thenTry under an explicit Executor, so sequential and parallel composition are written as chains instead of blocking waits, while the write end stays explicit as folly::Promise::setValue. Choose it where several pending values must be combined without moving the code base to C++20 coroutines, or where a framework already hands out this Future type.
pitfalls: Continuations run on the executor you name, so forgetting via() runs callbacks inline on whichever thread settled the future, and mixing executors silently changes ordering.
Chain failures surface at the get()/wait point (or as a broken promise), not at the producer - a chain that drops the exception loses the failure the same way an ignored future does.
